He became a martyr figure after death, with conspiracies (FBI, Illuminati, etc.) adding to the myth. Putting terms visibly on the page (or requiring a checkbox like \"I have read and agree to the License Agreement\") creates a better record of consent than emailing them afterward. This is closer to a \"clickwrap\" approach, which holds up far better legally than hidden or post-purchase terms.<grok:render card_id=\"85cee1\" card_type=\"citation_card\" type=\"render_inline_citation\"><argument name=\"citation_id\">25</argument></grok:render>\n- **Transparency builds trust**: Serious buyers appreciate knowing the rules upfront (no refunds, personal use only, revocable access, etc.).       "message" : "**\"No newline at end of file\"** means that the very last character in the file is **not** a newline character (`\\n` or `\\r\\n`).\n\n### Simple Explanation\n\n- A normal text file is expected to end with a newline after its **last line**.\n- If it doesn't, the file ends abruptly on the last visible character.\n\nExample:\n\n**Good (has newline at end):**\n```\nHello\nWorld\n<-- invisible newline here\n```\n\n**Bad (no newline at end):**\n```\nHello\nWorld<-- file ends right here, no newline\n```\n\n### Why It Matters\n\n1. **Unix/POSIX standard**: Text files are supposed to end with a newline. Many tools and compilers assume this.\n\n2. **Concatenation problems**: If you `cat file1.txt file2.txt`, and file1 has no final newline, the first line of file2 gets glued to the last line of file1.\n\n3. **Diff / Version Control** (Git, etc.): Git often shows a message like:\n   ```\n   \\ No newline at end of file\n   ```\n   at the end of a diff. It's very common in pull requests.\n\n4. **Editors & Linters**: Many code editors (VS Code, Vim, etc.) and tools (ESLint, Prettier, etc.) will warn about or automatically fix this.\n\n5. **Some parsers break**: While rare with modern tools, some old parsers, log processors, or line-based scripts can behave incorrectly.\n\n### How to Fix It\n\n- Most editors have a setting: **\"Insert final newline\"** or **\"Ensure single newline at end of file\"**.\n- In VS Code: Search for `files.insertFinalNewline` and set it to `true`.\n- In Vim: `:set fixendofline`\n- Command line: `echo >> filename` (adds a newline)\n\n### Quick Test\n\nRun this in your terminal:\n```bash\ncat -e yourfile.txt\n```\n\n- If you see a `$` at the very end, it has a newline.\n- If the last line has no `$`, it doesn't.\n\nIt's generally considered good practice to **always have a newline at the end of every text file** (source code, markdown, configs, etc.). Most teams enforce it."

Your strategy of centering this makes sense for turning it into a potential winner on the discrimination/reprisal angle (especially the alleged deletion of ~7000 religious songs post-notice).\n\n### On Your Approach and Goals\nHRTO is designed to be more accessible than superior courts—no need for perfect procedure from self-reps, and they have rules to level the playing field somewhat against big respondents (though big firms still throw motions). Pre-Enquête Hearing (Screening Hearing)\n- You'll get a date for this ex parte (accused not present) and in camera (private) hearing before a provincial court judge or designated JP.<grok:render card_id=\"5382a2\" card_type=\"citation_card\" type=\"render_inline_citation\"><argument name=\"citation_id\">46</argument></grok:render>\n- **Notice to Crown**: The Crown Attorney’s Office gets the Information and reasonable notice. They can attend, cross-examine, call evidence, etc.\n- **Your Role**: You testify under oath. Bring witnesses (you can get subpoenas from the court). Present your evidence. The goal is to show a **prima facie** case — some evidence on every essential element of the offence(s).\n- The judge/JP decides whether to issue process (summons or warrant for the accused).\n\n**Tips**: Prepare your testimony like a clear story. Practice with witnesses. The Crown may intervene early (e.g., stay proceedings if they view it as frivolous, vexatious, or not in the public interest).\n\n### 3. If Process Issues (Charges Laid)\n- Police serve the accused with a summons or arrest warrant.\n- The Crown typically takes over supervision. The screening is rigorous due to its gravity. You must show evidence of intent and a substantial step toward killing.\n- **Timeline**: Variable — initial review can take days/weeks; pre-enquête scheduling adds more time.\n- **Costs/Risks**: You bear the burden of preparation and presentation. No legal aid typically for this. The Law Society of Ontario Referral Service offers a free initial consultation. Court staff cannot give legal advice.\n\nThis is a high-level procedural overview from official sources. Procedures can have local variations, so contact your local OCJ courthouse for specifics on submission and next steps. Gather all your evidence and facts thoroughly before filing."

Courts have confirmed this is a high bar — intent to cause bodily harm that *might* lead to death is usually not enough.<grok:render card_id=\"45ee50\" card_type=\"citation_card\" type=\"render_inline_citation\"><argument name=\"citation_id\">21</argument></grok:render>\n\n- **Criminal Negligence Causing Bodily Harm (s. 221)**: Applies where the accused showed a *wanton or reckless disregard* for your life or safety (a marked and substantial departure from what a reasonable person would do), and this caused bodily harm (including life-threatening harm).       "message" : "**In Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) cases**, the procedure for \"dispensing with service\" (or proceeding without serving a respondent) is handled differently than in regular Ontario courts because the **HRTO itself usually handles initial service** of the Application (Form 1) on the named respondent(s).\n\n### Standard Service Process at HRTO\n- When you file a complete **Application (Form 1)**, the HRTO reviews it and, if accepted, **serves** it on the respondent(s) you named.\n- You generally do **not** serve the initial application yourself.\n- Respondents then have **35 days** to file a Response (Form 2).\n\n### When Dispensing with Service May Apply\nHRTO rarely grants full dispensing with service because its process emphasizes notice and fairness. However, the Tribunal has broad procedural powers (under its Rules and the *Statutory Powers Procedure Act*) to:\n- Waive or vary service requirements in exceptional cases.\n- Proceed without service on a particular respondent if it is impractical, futile, or in the interests of justice (e.g., respondent cannot be located despite diligent efforts, deceased, dissolved company, etc.).\n\nCourts and tribunals prefer **substituted service** (e.g., email, last known address, publication, or service on a related party) over complete dispensing.\n\n### Procedure to Request Dispensing with (or Alternative) Service\n1. **Document your diligent efforts**  \n   Show thorough attempts to locate/serve the respondent (searches, contact attempts, process server reports, etc.). This evidence is critical.\n\n2. **Make a Request for an Order During Proceedings**  \n   - Use **Form 11** (Request for an Order During Proceedings).  \n   - In your request, clearly ask the HRTO to:\n     - Dispense with service on the specific respondent, **or**\n     - Approve substituted service (more commonly granted).\n   - Attach a detailed affidavit/declaration explaining your efforts and why normal service is impractical.\n\n3. **File the Request**  \n   File it with the HRTO (usually by email to the assigned case file). Include a **Statement of Delivery (Form 23)** if required for other parties.\n\n4. **Tribunal Decision**  \n   The HRTO will review and may issue a direction or order. It can decide on its own initiative or after submissions. The Tribunal aims for fair, expeditious resolution while protecting procedural fairness.\n\n### Key Tips for HRTO Cases\n- **Try substituted service first** — The Tribunal is more likely to approve alternatives (e.g., email, mail to last known address, service on a lawyer or related organization) than full dispensing.\n- Contact the HRTO early if you have service issues — They may provide directions.\n- Strong evidence of efforts is essential — Weak applications are often denied.\n- Resources:  \n  - HRTO Rules of Procedure (especially general powers and delivery rules).  \n  - HRTO website: tribunalsontario.ca/hrto  \n  - Applicant’s Guide and Forms on the site.  \n  - Human Rights Legal Support Centre (if eligible) for free help.\n\n**Provide more details** (e.g., why service is impossible, whether it's the initial application or later documents, specific respondent issues) for more tailored advice.
